Same pattern, new paper: a hospital or clinic bill.
A medical bill can be hard to read. Explainer will help you understand what you're looking at before you pay.
A bill from a hospital, a clinic, a doctor's office, or a collection agency, and how to tell them apart.
Which provider sent it, and which insurance plan, if any, was billed.
The date of the visit, the statement date, and the due date printed on the bill.
The total, what insurance has paid so far, and the amount the bill says is yours. Explainer points to the numbers on your bill and never estimates them.
Ask for an itemized bill, ask about financial help or a payment plan, or check it against your insurance paperwork.

Same pattern, new paper: a letter from your health insurance.

An explanation of benefits (EOB), a denial letter, an approval, or a request for information.
Which plan sent it: a plan through work, Covered California, Medi-Cal, or a school plan.
The date of service, the date on the letter, and any deadline the letter gives to respond.
What the plan paid, what it did not cover, and the amount it says you may owe. Explainer points to the numbers and never estimates them.
Compare it with the provider's bill, call the member number on your insurance card, or ask how to appeal.
Match the claim on the letter to the bill it belongs to before paying anything.

Look next to the violation code on your ticket. Is "Misdemeanor" checked, or does it say "Must appear"?
Yes, it says Misdemeanor or Must appear.
No, it says Infraction.
I can't tell.
This one box decides whether you can handle it online or have to go to court in person. Most people never hear that a traffic stop can be a misdemeanor.

Not yet, it's coming up.

Why Explainer asks:
California courts can lower fines, set up payment plans, or allow community service. Explainer never asks your income, just how it feels, so it can point you to the right option.
Here's your plan.
You've got this. Here's what's going on.
Your next move.
Put your court date in your phone right now, and plan to be at the courthouse in person.
For a misdemeanor, talking to a lawyer is worth it. If you can't afford one, ask the court about a public defender when you appear.
What this is.
A serious ticket. You have to go to court.

If the officer marked it as a misdemeanor, or the ticket says you must appear, this is more serious than a regular traffic ticket. You usually can't just pay it online. You have to go to court on your date.
Your date.
Type the date from your ticket. Explainer counts the days.
Due date or court date.
Watch out for.
Missing a court date you promised to appear for can be its own separate misdemeanor (Vehicle Code § 40508). This is the most expensive mistake people make.
Where this comes from.
Every rule above comes from an official source, checked Nov 22, 2026.
Your court date passed. Act today.

Missing your date doesn't make the ticket go away. If you promised to appear and didn't, that can become its own separate misdemeanor (Vehicle Code § 40508). The fix is still the same: contact the court as soon as you can. Courts see this all the time.
This is a good time to talk to a lawyer. If you can't afford one, ask the court about a public defender.
Call or go to the court named on your ticket today, and ask what to do about your missed date.
A misdemeanor usually can't be handled online, so don't wait for a letter or try to pay on a website. The court clerk can tell you what your next step is.

Question 7 of 7.
Look up your ticket and choose traffic school before your due date.

A regular ticket. Not criminal, but it has a deadline.

This is a traffic infraction, the most common kind of ticket. It's handled by the Superior Court of Los Angeles County. Long Beach tickets go to the LA County court system, not the City of Long Beach. You are not in criminal trouble, but you do have to deal with it by the date on your ticket.
Your options.
Traffic school.
Good fit for you.
Keeps it off your public record. Once every 18 months.
You pay the full amount plus a court fee and the school's own fee, then take a DMV-approved class. The ticket stays confidential, off your public record.
Source: California Rules of Court, Rule 4.104.
Ask to lower the amount.
Ask for less, a payment plan, or more time.

If paying would be hard, ask the court for a lower amount, a payment plan, more time, or community service. You can do it online with MyCitations. You'll be asked to enter a plea, so if you plan to fight the ticket, don't ask for a reduction first.
Source: California Courts Self-Help Guide: Ask to lower your fine (MyCitations).
Fight it.
Plead not guilty, in person or in writing.

If you believe you didn't do it, you can plead not guilty and have a trial in person, or a trial by written declaration, where you send your side in writing. For a written trial you usually pay the amount up front and get it back if you win.
Source: California Courts Self-Help Guide: Trial by written declaration.
Just pay it.
Fastest, but it goes on your driving record.
The fastest way to close it. It counts as a conviction, goes on your driving record, and can raise your insurance.
Source: California Courts Self-Help Guide: Traffic tickets.
The court's notice goes to the address on your ticket. If that's your parents' house, check the court website yourself so you aren't surprised.
Traffic school is not a free pass. You still pay the full amount, plus a court fee, plus the school.
The court will never text, call, or email you asking for payment. Only pay on the court's own website.
Explainer doesn't show fine amounts. The real amount is on your court notice or the court website, and it's often much higher than the base fine because of added fees.
First ask for traffic school. Then, if the amount is too much, ask the court to lower it with MyCitations.
Order matters: the state's guide says to ask for traffic school before you ask for a reduction.
Decide by your due date: pay it, or fight it if you believe you didn't do it.

Probably not for you.

If nothing shows up yet, that's normal. The court mails a notice with your amount and options, and it can take 30 days or longer. Your ticket may also show a date to appear. Don't wait for the letter if that date is coming.

Question 3 of 5.
Fix the problem, then get the proof of correction signed before your date.
The back of your ticket says who can sign it off. Then you send the signed proof to the court with the fee.
A fix-it ticket: fix it, prove it, pay a small fee.

A fix-it ticket (also called a correctable violation) means the officer saw something you can fix, like a broken light or expired tags. If you fix it and show proof, you usually just pay a small fee instead of the full fine.
Show proof and pay the fee.
Fix it, get it signed off, pay a small fee.
Fix it, get it signed off, and send the proof to the court with the small fee by your date.
Contest it like any other ticket.
If you don't think the ticket is right, you can contest it like any other ticket.

A city parking ticket, not a court case.

Question 3 of 3.
Have you seen the unit in person?
Not yet.
It's much easier to get a problem fixed, or written down, before you sign.
Before you pay an application fee, ask for an itemized receipt.
The landlord has to give you one. They also can't charge the fee when they know there's no unit available.
You're applying. Know what you can be charged.
Before offering you a lease, a landlord can check your application and may charge a screening fee. That fee has a legal maximum, and you are owed an itemized receipt.
What to check.
The application fee.
Limited by law, and you get a receipt.

An application screening fee has a legal maximum that changes each year. The landlord must give you a receipt that itemizes the cost. They can't charge it when they know, or should know, there is no vacancy.
Source: California Department of Real Estate, Landlords' and Tenants' Rights Guide: Looking for a Rental Unit.
A holding deposit.
It only holds the unit for a set time.

A holding deposit only guarantees the landlord won't rent the unit to someone else for a stated time. Ask whether it goes toward your first month's rent or your security deposit, and get the agreement and a receipt in writing.
What a landlord can't ask.
In most cases, not your immigration or citizenship status.

In most cases a landlord may not ask about your immigration or citizenship status. They can still ask for documents that confirm who you are and that you can pay. Landlords are also not allowed to refuse you because you receive Section 8 assistance, with a narrow exception for renting one room in a home the owner lives in.
Never pay rent in cash without getting a receipt, every single time.
Every rule above comes from an official source, checked Nov 26, 2026.
See the unit before you pay a deposit.
Walk through the actual unit first. Anything the landlord promises to fix should end up written into the agreement.
Does the agreement have an end date?
Yes, a set term.
Like 6 or 12 months.
No, it's month to month.
A set term and a month-to-month agreement work differently if the rent changes or you want to leave.
Besides your first month's rent, how much are you asked to pay up front?
One month's rent or less.
More than one month's rent.
Count deposits, last month's rent, and pet, key or cleaning fees.
I'm not sure yet.
California limits the security deposit for most rentals. Explainer asks so it can tell you what to check. It never asks what you earn.
Read every page before you sign, and get every promise in writing.
If the landlord said they would fix or include something, it should be in the agreement. You don't have to sign on the spot.
A lease with a set term. Read it before you sign.

A lease or rental agreement is a contract. Yours has a set term. During that term the landlord can't raise the rent unless the agreement allows it, and if you move out early you can still owe rent. Read every page and make sure you understand it. You don't have to sign on the spot.
The deposit.
One month's rent at most, for most rentals.

Since July 1, 2024, most landlords can charge no more than one month's rent as a security deposit. Last month's rent, and pet, key or cleaning fees, all count as the deposit. Small landlords can charge up to two months' rent. A landlord can't require a deposit to be nonrefundable.
Source: California Department of Real Estate, Landlords' and Tenants' Rights Guide: When You Have Decided to Rent.
How you pay rent.
Cash only, or online only, usually isn't allowed.
A landlord normally can't make you pay rent in cash, or only by electronic transfer. You must be allowed another way, such as a personal check, a money order or a cashier's check.
Source: California Department of Real Estate, Landlords' and Tenants' Rights Guide: Living in the Rental Unit.
Late fees.
A late fee can't be a penalty.
A late fee that is so high it works as a penalty is not legally valid. A reasonable late fee may be. Find the late fee line in your agreement so it doesn't surprise you.
Move-in photos.
Photos of the unit protect your deposit.

For tenancies that begin on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord has to take photos of the unit. You can ask for copies, or take your own before you move your things in. A move-in checklist isn't required by law, but it's good practice to fill one out with the landlord, then sign and date it.
Your signed copy.
You're owed one within 15 days of signing.
The landlord must give you a signed copy of the agreement within 15 days of signing. Keep it somewhere you can find it.
Source: California Department of Real Estate, Landlords' and Tenants' Rights Guide: Before You Agree to Rent.
In most cases a landlord may not ask about your immigration or citizenship status.
Your basic rights as a tenant stay in place no matter what the agreement says.
Long Beach has a Just Cause ordinance that covers tenants who have lived in the unit 12 months or more. Some homes are excluded.
See the unit before you sign.
Walk through the actual unit first. Anything the landlord promises to fix should be written into the agreement.
See the unit in person before you sign or pay anything.

Check the deposit before you pay.
Since July 1, 2024, most landlords can charge no more than one month's rent as a security deposit. Last month's rent, and pet, key or cleaning fees, all count as the deposit.
Small landlords can charge up to two months' rent. That means an individual, or an LLC owned by individuals, who owns and rents one or two properties with no more than four rental units.
Before you pay, ask the landlord in writing how the total fits California's deposit limit.
You're not accusing anyone. Some small landlords are allowed two months' rent. Asking in writing gets you a clear answer you can keep.
A month-to-month agreement. Read it before you sign.
A lease or rental agreement is a contract. Yours runs month to month, with no set end date. Read every page and make sure you understand it. You don't have to sign on the spot.
A lease is a contract. Read it before you sign.

"Lease" and "rental agreement" mean the same thing. Look for whether yours has an end date, which makes it a set term, or runs month to month. Read every page and make sure you understand it. You don't have to sign on the spot.
Get your signed copy, and take dated photos before you move your things in.
The landlord owes you a signed copy within 15 days of signing. Photos of how the unit looks now protect your deposit when you move out.
You've signed. Here's what you're owed now.

Your agreement is a contract, and both sides are held to it. With a set term, the landlord can't raise the rent during the term unless the agreement allows it. If you move out early, you can still owe rent. Your basic rights as a tenant stay in place no matter what the agreement says.
Getting your deposit back.
Within 21 days of moving out.
Within 21 days of moving out, the landlord must return your deposit, minus lawful deductions, and give you an itemized statement. A landlord can't require a deposit to be nonrefundable.
Source: California Attorney General: Landlord-Tenant Issues.
After 12 months in the unit, state law gives most renters eviction protections and limits how much the rent can go up in a year. Some homes are excluded.

Mismo patrón, nuevo papel: tu primer contrato.
Un contrato de renta es un acuerdo serio. Así es como Explainer te guiará línea por línea antes de firmar.
Cómo funcionará esta guía de Explainer.
Cada guía de Explainer hace las mismas seis preguntas clave. Solo cambian las reglas y opciones.
1. ¿Qué es este papel?
Contrato a plazo fijo vs. mes a mes, y quién aparece realmente en el contrato.
2. ¿Dónde queda el lugar?
Long Beach, Condado de LA o el resto de California. Las reglas locales importan.
3. ¿Qué fecha importa?
Fecha de mudanza, fin del contrato y cuándo empiezan las ventanas de aviso.
4. ¿Qué te puede costar?
Renta mensual, límites del depósito, recargos por retraso y qué servicios pagas.
5. ¿Cuáles son tus opciones?
Pedir cambios por escrito, tomar fotos al entrar o decidir no firmar todavía.
6. Tu próximo paso.
Una revisión clara antes de firmar o enviar tu primer depósito.
Esta guía se activa solo después de verificar cada regla.
